prompt: What has to be done to a container before its change feed can be read in the default mode?
hint: `feed.py` created the container and read the feed at once.

choices.text: Enable a change feed policy with a retention period
choices.why: That is for all versions and deletes, the other mode.

choices.text: Nothing
choices.why: Right: every container has one.

choices.text: Turn on continuous backup for the account
choices.why: Also the other mode's requirement on Azure.

choices.text: Create a lease container beside it
choices.why: Leases are for the change feed processor; `feed.py` used none.

prompt: Changes for customers `c-7` and `c-8` are written in that order. In what order does the feed return them?
hint: Where is order guaranteed?

choices.text: `c-7` then `c-8`, in the order they were written
choices.why: Only changes to the same partition key keep their order.

choices.text: Either order, per key, not between keys
choices.why: Right: the order holds inside a partition key and nowhere else.

choices.text: By `_ts`, across the whole container
choices.why: There is no container-wide order to rely on.

choices.text: Alphabetically by id within each page
choices.why: Ids have nothing to do with the feed's order.

prompt: What is inside the continuation token `feed.py` decoded?
hint: Look at the line that starts with `continuation:`.

choices.text: The ids of the items already read
choices.why: It records positions, not items.

choices.text: A signed timestamp the server checks
choices.why: It is base64-encoded JSON anybody can decode.

choices.text: The position reached in each feed range
choices.why: Right: one range from '' to FF on the emulator, at position 5.

choices.text: The session token of the last write
choices.why: Related numbers, a different token for a different purpose.

prompt: Match each starting point to where the feed starts.
hint: One description fits none.

pairs.right: The oldest entry the feed still has
The next change after the request
The first change at or after that time
Just after the position it records

right_distractors: The last change of each item, newest first

prompt: `feed.py` made three creates, two updates and one delete. How many entries did the feed return from the beginning?
hint: One per living item, as it is now.

prompt: A view built from the latest-version feed still shows an order that was deleted last week. Why?
hint: What did the feed say about `o-2`?

choices.text: Deletes are not in that feed, so nothing said so
choices.why: Right: mark it deleted first, and let a time to live remove it.

choices.text: The processor's token is a week old
choices.why: An old token would replay changes, but a delete is not among them.

choices.text: The feed reports deletes only after the time to live
choices.why: In this mode it never reports a delete.

choices.text: Deletes are reported once a day, in a batch
choices.why: No such batch exists.

prompt: Put in order the soft delete of `softdelete.py`.
hint: The readers have to see it before it goes.
items: Set `deleted` to true and give it a `ttl`
Write it back, which puts it in the feed
Readers of the feed remove it from their views
The time to live removes it from the container

prompt: A nightly job reads the feed of the orders container and may be down for a weekend. What `ttl` should a soft-deleted order get?
hint: Whom is the `ttl` a promise to?

choices.text: 5 seconds, as in `softdelete.py`
choices.why: Five seconds is a number for a lesson.

choices.text: None: the job reads the flag whenever it next runs
choices.why: Without a ttl the item stays for ever; with too short a one the job never sees the flag.

choices.text: Several days, longer than any reader's absence
choices.why: Right: an item that expires before a reader sees the mark is a delete that reader never learns about.

choices.text: One day, the default of a container with time to live on
choices.why: `default_ttl=-1` gives items no time to live at all unless they carry one.

prompt: Why does `processor.py` save the view before the checkpoint, and not the other way round?
hint: Imagine a crash between the two, in each order.

choices.text: Because Azurite writes blobs in alphabetical order
choices.why: The order is the program's, and it matters wherever the blobs are.

choices.text: The other order would skip changes the view never got, for good
choices.why: Right: this order repeats some changes, and loses none.

choices.text: Because the token is only valid once the view exists
choices.why: The token is valid on its own; the risk is what it skips.

choices.text: To make the feed deliver every change exactly once
choices.why: It makes delivery at least once; the view is what makes a repeat harmless.

prompt: After the crash and the next run, what did `processor.py` show for customer `c-8`, in reais?
hint: The change was applied twice.

prompt: A colleague changes `processor.py` to keep one running total per customer and add each order's amount to it. What happens on the run after a crash before the checkpoint?
hint: The same changes are read again.

choices.text: Nothing: the feed does not repeat changes
choices.why: The feed resumes from the old token, so it does.

choices.text: The run fails, because the token is out of date
choices.why: An old token is a valid token; it just points further back.

choices.text: The library notices the repeat and skips it
choices.why: Nothing in the library tracks what your program applied.

choices.text: The orders read again are added twice
choices.why: Right: adding is not idempotent, setting is.

prompt: Delivery that never loses a change but may repeat one is called at-least-___ delivery.
hint: How many times, at least?

prompt: What did `versions.py` get for the delete of `o-6`?
hint: Look at the last line.

choices.text: Nothing, as in latest version
choices.why: This mode keeps deletes.

choices.text: Its previous version
choices.why: Right: an entry with no current item, `delete`, now None, before `packed`.

choices.text: The item as it was created
choices.why: The delete's previous image is the last version, `packed`.

choices.text: An error, because the item no longer exists
choices.why: The feed reports the delete; nothing is read from the container.

prompt: Which are true of the all versions and deletes mode? Choose all that apply.
hint: One is true of latest version only.

choices.text: It has to be switched on for the container
choices.why: Right: the `orders` container without a policy refused it.

choices.text: It keeps changes only for a retention period
choices.why: Right: on Azure the continuous backup period, on the emulator 1 to 10 minutes.

choices.text: It starts from now or from a token, not from the beginning
choices.why: Right: the history exists only from when it was switched on.

choices.text: It returns each item once, as it is now
choices.why: That is latest version; this mode returns every step.

prompt: The emulator accepted a retention of 10 minutes and refused 60. What does that tell you about Azure?
hint: Whose rule was it?

choices.text: That Azure keeps changes for 10 minutes at most
choices.why: On Azure retention follows the continuous backup period.

choices.text: Nothing; the limit is the emulator's
choices.why: Right, and nothing in this course measured Azure's.

choices.text: That Azure counts the retention in hours
choices.why: The refusal says nothing about Azure's units.

choices.text: That 60 minutes needs a support request on Azure
choices.why: Nothing documented says so.

prompt: What does the lease container hold?
hint: `processor.py` kept the same thing in a blob, minus one field.

choices.text: A copy of every change, for replay
choices.why: The changes stay in the monitored container's feed.

choices.text: The view the delegate builds
choices.why: The view is wherever your delegate writes it.

choices.text: Owners and tokens
choices.why: Right: per feed range, its owner and its continuation token; a lease is a checkpoint with an owner written on it.

choices.text: The list of instances allowed to read
choices.why: Instances take leases; nobody lists them in advance.

prompt: A second instance of a change feed processor starts. What happens?
hint: Leases are shared out.

choices.text: The leases are rebalanced, and each range is read by one instance
choices.why: Right: that is what the leases are for.

choices.text: Both instances read every range, and the delegate sees each change twice
choices.why: That is `processor.py` started twice, without leases.

choices.text: The second waits until the first stops
choices.why: Instances share the work while both run.

choices.text: The monitored container's throughput doubles
choices.why: Throughput is set on the container, not by its readers.

prompt: Which of these is true of the Azure Functions Cosmos DB trigger?
hint: It is the change feed processor with hosting.

choices.text: It delivers each change exactly once
choices.why: It is at-least-once, like the processor it is built on.

choices.text: It needs no lease container
choices.why: It needs the same lease container.

choices.text: It is how Python programs read the feed with leases
choices.why: It is a hosting option, not a Python library feature.

choices.text: It runs at most one instance per lease
choices.why: Right: one lease is read by one instance at a time.

prompt: Quitanda adds a search index, a copy to the lake and the spend view, each as its own consumer of the orders feed. What does that cost in reads?
hint: Each consumer has its own leases.

choices.text: One read of the feed, shared by all three
choices.why: Each reads independently, at its own pace.

choices.text: Three reads, from the orders container
choices.why: Right: each consumer pays for its own pages, from the same throughput the application uses.

choices.text: Three reads, billed to the lease containers
choices.why: Leases cost little; the feed's pages are charged to the monitored container.

choices.text: Nothing extra: reading the feed is free
choices.why: Every page of the feed costs request units.

prompt: Finance wants every status an order passed through, with its time, for the last month. What do you build?
hint: Latest version drops steps; the other mode keeps them for a limited time.

choices.text: A reader of the latest-version feed that polls every minute
choices.why: Two changes inside one minute still collapse into one.

choices.text: A query on `_ts` over the orders container
choices.why: `_ts` is the last write's time; the earlier steps are gone.

choices.text: An all-versions consumer that keeps every entry
choices.why: Right, or a status history kept in the item itself; the feed alone keeps changes only for its retention.

choices.text: A soft delete with a ttl of one month
choices.why: That keeps deleted items around; it does not record steps.

prompt: Which of these make a feed consumer safe to run twice on the same change? Choose all that apply.
hint: Setting, not adding.

choices.text: Writing the view keyed by the order id
choices.why: Right: the second write sets the same value.

choices.text: Removing an order flagged deleted, if present
choices.why: Right: removing what is already gone changes nothing.

choices.text: Adding each order's amount to a running total
choices.why: The repeat adds again.

choices.text: Saving the checkpoint before the view
choices.why: That loses changes; it does not make repeats safe.

prompt: Where does a Python program running on Azure keep its place in the feed, with version 4.17.1 of the library?
hint: The library has no processor.

choices.text: In a lease container the library manages
choices.why: That is the .NET and Java processor.

choices.text: Nowhere: the service remembers each reader
choices.why: The service remembers nothing about readers.

choices.text: Wherever the program saves the continuation token
choices.why: Right: a blob, as in `processor.py`, or a document of its own.

choices.text: In the `_lsn` of the last item it read
choices.why: One `_lsn` is one partition's position; the token covers every range.
